qs.q: During a regional nerve block of the pelvic floor, an anatomical bony landmark is palpated transvaginally to locate the pudendal nerve. Which structure serves as this landmark?
o: The greater trochanter of the femur
The pubic tubercle of the pelvic bone
The ischial spine of the pelvic bone
The ischial tuberosity of the bone
qs.e: The pudendal nerve crosses the sacrospinous ligament just medial to the ischial spine, making it the key landmark.

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman is being assessed for the reversal of a temporary loop ileostomy. Which clinical finding must be confirmed regarding her pelvic floor function before proceeding with closure?
qs.e: Before closing a temporary stoma, it is vital to confirm that anal sphincter function is adequate to prevent postoperative incontinence. Fasting blood glucose is relevant for diabetes control but does not test pelvic floor continence.
qs.s: Intestinal Stomas: Colostomy and Ileostomy, Types, Care and: MCQs

qs.q: During a repair of a pelvic floor defect, a surgeon identifies the deep perineal fascia. With which anatomical structure of the anterior abdominal wall is this layer directly continuous?
qs.e: The deep perineal fascia (Colles' fascia) is continuous with Scarpa's fascia of the anterior abdominal wall, allowing the potential spread of extravasated urine. The other options misstate its attachments or superficial relationships.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The pelvic floor is a muscular diaphragm that supports pelvic organs, maintains continence, and contributes to core stability. Weakness or injury can cause prolapse, incontinence, and pain.

sections.p: The pelvic floor forms the base of the pelvis, separating the abdominal cavity from the perineum. It consists of muscles, fascia, and ligaments that work together to support viscera and control sphincters.
b: Key muscles: levator ani (pubococcygeus, puborectalis, iliococcygeus) and coccygeus
Functions: organ support, continence, sexual function, posture

sections.p: The levator ani originates from the pubic bone, ischial spine, and tendinous arch of the obturator internus, inserting into the coccyx and anococcygeal raphe.
b: Divided into right and left halves, forming a sling around the anal canal
Coccygeus lies posterior to levator ani, anchoring to the sacrum

sections.p: Anteriorly the pelvic floor lies behind the bladder and urethra; laterally it borders the obturator internus fascia; posteriorly it contacts the rectum and anal canal.
b: Broad ligament, ureters, ovaries, fallopian tubes run lateral to the floor
Internal iliac vessels pass just above the floor

sections.p: Arterial blood comes from the inferior gluteal artery, branches of the internal pudendal artery, and the middle rectal artery.
b: Venous drainage follows the internal iliac veins
Rich anastomoses help maintain tissue health

sections.p: Motor innervation is primarily via the pudendal nerve (S2‑S4) and direct branches from the sacral plexus; sensory fibers travel with the same nerves.
b: Pudendal nerve injury leads to incontinence and perineal pain
Pelvic splanchnic nerves contribute autonomic control

sections.p: The floor maintains organ position, provides continence by supporting the urethral and anal sphincters, and assists in intra‑abdominal pressure regulation during coughing, lifting, and defecation.
b: Puborectalis creates the anorectal angle for continence
Levator ani contracts during Valsalva to prevent descent

sections.p: Weakness or denervation of the pelvic floor leads to prolapse, stress urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence, and chronic pelvic pain. Trauma, childbirth, chronic cough, and heavy lifting are common causes.
b: Stress urinary incontinence: urethral hypermobility from levator laxity
Pelvic organ prolapse: descent of bladder, uterus, or rectum on bearing down
Denervation: pudendal neuropathy from prolonged lithotomy or obstetric injury

t.b: Detects organ descent; a positive descent confirms pelvic floor weakness
Distinguishes stress vs urge incontinence; abnormal leak pressure indicates sphincter deficiency
Visualizes muscle bulk and defects; unavailable → use bedside ultrasound or clinical staging

sections.p: During a rectal or vaginal exam, ask the patient to bear down. Observe for perineal descent, rectocele, or cystocele. Palpate the levator ani for tone and defects.
b: Positive perineal descent suggests levator ani denervation
A wide puborectalis angle indicates fecal incontinence risk

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of pelvic pain with fever (possible infection)

faq.q: Why does bearing down reveal pelvic floor weakness?
faq.a: Increased intra‑abdominal pressure stresses the floor; a weak floor allows visible descent of perineal structures.

faq.q: Can pelvic floor exercises improve prolapse?
faq.a: Yes, targeted levator ani strengthening can reduce mild prolapse and improve continence.

faq.q: Is pelvic floor dysfunction more common after childbirth?
faq.a: Yes, vaginal delivery stretches and can injure the levator ani and pudendal nerve, increasing risk of incontinence and prolapse.
